extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political science; analysts of party systems and comparative politics
extracted.subtask_description: Identification and evaluation of features, organization, incentives, and behaviour of political parties and politicians (primarily in the United States) as described in a political-science textbook excerpt.

rubrics_metrics.name: National party viability: avoid sectionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: There is at present a strong feeling in America against any sentiment or organization which relies on or appeals to one particular region of the country... By the mere fact of its springing from a local root, and urging a local interest, a party would set the rest of the country against it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party based on a single region, race, religion, or trade is likely to be insignificant as a national party and will be 'self-condemned in American eyes.' Examples/anti-patterns: a national party founded on the exclusion of Chinese/Japanese would be insignificant nationally; an Irish, German, or Roman Catholic party running sectional candidates would be rejected; trade-based parties may succeed temporarily in a State but become ridiculous when trying to become national.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage local factions by bargaining votes rather than running nationally
rubrics_metrics.description: If a local or sectional group is content to remain a mere opinion or demand, not attacking either national party, but willing to bestow the votes it can control on whichever will meet its wishes, it is powerful, because the two great parties will bid against one another for its support by flatteries and concessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical advice for local interests: exert disproportionate influence by withholding independent national organization and instead offering votes to major parties; illustration: anti-Asian sentiment on the Pacific coast produced promises and anti-Asiatic legislation from both parties when those local votes mattered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements to found a new national party
rubrics_metrics.description: To influence the votes, even to reach the ears, of a population of ninety millions of people, is an undertaking to be entered on only when some really great cause fires the national imagination, disposes the people to listen, persuades the wealthy to spend freely of their substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Founding a viable national party is costly and time-consuming (example: six years to build the Republican party). Attempts without broad causes/funding (examples: 1872 independent party, 1884 Independent Republicans/Mugwumps) have failed. Implication: new parties require sustained organization, national appeal, and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party decision-making processes: conventions, platforms, caucuses
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief thing is the selection of candidates. This is done in party meetings called conventions. When a party has a policy, it is settled in a convention and declared in a document called a platform. Party tactics in Congress are decided on by meetings of the party in each House of Congress called caucuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational standard: use conventions to select candidates and settle policy, issue a platform as the party's declaration, and use legislative caucuses to coordinate tactics. Leaders influence these processes but may 'efface themselves' respecting equality and to avoid envy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue a platform even when no coherent policy exists
rubrics_metrics.description: When it has no policy, the platform is issued none the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A platform functions as the public declaration of the party; producing one is a routine output of party organization and important for signaling even in absence of coherent policy. Anti-pattern: failing to issue any platform undermines clarity of party position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for local office selection: honesty and businesslike care
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities and counties have not strictly speaking any political questions to deal with; their business is to pave and fight, to keep the streets clean, maintain an efficient police and well-barred prisons, administer the poor law and charitable institutions with integrity, judgment, and economy. Hence at city and county elections the main objects ought to be to choose honest and careful men of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For municipal offices prioritize administrative competence, integrity, economy, and judgement over party ideology; party label 'need make no difference' to concrete municipal action. Anti-pattern: bringing national party tenets to bear on routine municipal administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build federated party organization from local to national
rubrics_metrics.description: Every circumscription of State and local government... has a regular Republican party organization... and each federated, so to speak, to the larger organizations above it, represented in them and working for them in drilling and energizing the party within the area which is the sphere of its action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational principle: effective parties have local organizations that are integrated (federated) into larger structures so they can mobilize voters, drill activists, and represent local interests upward. Implementation: maintain regular local party machinery that feeds into state and national levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainment of party machinery requires constant local vigilance and labour
rubrics_metrics.description: The shortness of terms of office, and the large number of offices filled by election, make elections very frequent... Constant vigilance, constant exertions on the spot, are needed. The list of voters must be incessantly looked after, newly-admitted or newly-settled citizens enrolled, the active local men frequently consulted and kept in good humour, meetings arranged for, tickets for all vacant offices agreed upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational criteria for party maintenance: continuous voter registration work, regular outreach to local activists, frequent organization of meetings and tickets. Consequence: the work is hard and dull and produces a need for dedicated workers (leading to professional politicians).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentive structure producing professional politicians: paid offices and patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: The inducement to undertake the dull and toilsome work of election politics... is the inducement of places in the public service. To make them attractive they must be paid... The holders of nearly all those administrative places... were, till recent years, liable to be dismissed whenever power changes from one party to another, so that those who belong to the party out of office have a direct chance of office when their party comes in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic criterion: remuneration, patronage, and the prospect of office make politics a livelihood and produce an 'Inner Circle' of professional politicians. Reform guidance: civil service reform reduces dismissals and thus lessens patronage-driven inducements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective leadership in the American context relies on the stump and national traversal
rubrics_metrics.description: The separation of the legislative from the executive department lowers the importance of leadership in parties... The President... does not always find it possible to direct the policy of his party... There remains the stump, and it is more by the stump than in any other way that an American statesman speaks to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for successful national leadership in the U.S.: use stump speeches and extensive travel to communicate directly to the electorate because parliamentary channels are weak for mass persuasion. Anti-pattern: relying on legislative prominence alone to shape national opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party discipline: trade-offs between cohesion and suppression of honest dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a sort of military discipline about party life which has its good as well as its bad side, for if it sometimes checks the expression of honest disapproval, it also restrains jealousy, abashes self-seeking, prevents recrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative evaluation: party discipline is valuable for order and preventing destructive factionalism but can stifle legitimate criticism; parties must balance cohesion with allowance for honest dissent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and composition of the 'Inner Circle' (professional politicians)
rubrics_metrics.description: In America the Inner Circle, that is to say, the persons who make political work the chief business of life, for the time being, includes: First. All members of both Houses of Congress. Secondly. All Federal office-holders except the judges... Thirdly. A large part of the members of State legislatures... Fourthly. Nearly all State office-holders... Fifthly. Nearly all holders of paid offices in the greater and in many of the smaller cities... Sixthly. A large number of people who hold no office but want to get one, or perhaps even who desire work under a municipality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to identify who counts as professional politicians in the U.S. context; estimate that this group numbers by hundreds of thousands and includes office-holders, expectants, and paid local operatives. Application: when analysing party dynamics, treat these categories as the core mobilizing class.
